nodes.name: Persistent homology with torsion
nodes.statement: The extension of the theory of Persistent Homology to the case of persistent homology groups with torsion is an important open problem.

nodes.name: Set of grasps
nodes.statement: Each grasp can be seen as an unordered pair $\{p,q\}$ of points on $\mathcal{S}$, and we can consider the set $\mathcal{G}$ of all possible grasps (endowed with the Hausdorff distance between unordered pairs).

nodes.name: Grasp cost function
nodes.statement: If the cost of the grasp is given by a value $\varphi_\mathcal{G}(\{p,q\})$, we are naturally led to the problem of comparing the similarity of the grasps possible for two different objects with surfaces $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{S}'$, with respect to the cost functions $\varphi_\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{G}\to \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi_{\mathcal{G}'}:\mathcal{G}'\to \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: The cost of a grasp $\{p,q\}$ is a real value $\varphi_\mathcal{G}(\{p,q\})$; comparing grasps of two objects is a comparison of cost functions.

nodes.name: Persistent homology groups of the grasp space
nodes.statement: In other words, we can consider the persistent homology groups ${H}_k^{(\mathcal{G},\varphi_\mathcal{G})}(u,v)$ given by the equivalence classes of cycles in ${H}_k(\mathcal{G}_v)$ that contain at least one cycle in $\mathcal{G}_u$, where $\mathcal{G}_t$ represents the set of points of $\mathcal{G}$ at which $\varphi_\mathcal{G}$ takes a value not greater than $t$.
nodes.statement_short: $H_k(u,v)$ = classes of cycles in $H_k(\mathcal{G}_v)$ containing a cycle in the sublevel set $\mathcal{G}_u$.

nodes.name: Torsion in the persistent homology of two-finger grasps of the sphere
nodes.statement: Let us assume that the cost of the grasp is given by the value $\varphi_\mathcal{G}(\{p,q\})=-\|p-q\|$, so relating the cost of a grasp to the level of closure of the robotic hand. For the sake of simplicity, let us examine the case $\mathcal{S}=S^2=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3:x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}$. In this case, the group ${H}_1^{(\mathcal{G},\varphi_\mathcal{G})}(u,v)$ has torsion, when $u<v<0$ and $u$ is close enough to zero.
assumptions: the cost of the grasp is given by the value $\varphi_\mathcal{G}(\{p,q\})=-\|p-q\|$
when $u<v<0$ and $u$ is close enough to zero
nodes.statement_short: For grasps of $S^2$ with cost $-\|p-q\|$, the persistent group $H_1(u,v)$ has torsion for $u<v<0$ near zero.

nodes.name: Proof of torsion for grasps of the sphere
nodes.statement: Indeed, we can consider the continuous function $f$ taking each unordered pair $\{p,q\}\in \mathcal{G}_v$ to the direction of the line $l$ through $p$ and $q$ (note that $\{p,q\}\in \mathcal{G}_v$ implies $p\neq q$, so that $l$ is well-defined). This direction can be seen as a point in the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$. Let us observe that, for $v$ close enough to zero, the function $f:\mathcal{G}_v\to \mathbb{RP}^2$ is a homotopy equivalence (the homotopy inverse of $f$ is the function $g:\mathbb{RP}^2\to \mathcal{G}_v$ that takes each direction $w$ to the unordered pair $\{p,q\}$, where $p$ and $q$ are the points at which the line through $(0,0,0)$, having direction $w$, meets $S^2$). Hence $f$ induces an isomorphism between the singular homology groups of $\mathcal{G}_v$ and $\mathbb{RP}^2$. As a consequence, since $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)$ has torsion, the persistent homology group ${H}_1^{(\mathcal{G},\varphi_\mathcal{G})}(u,v)$ has torsion, too, when $u$ is close enough to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Map pairs to line directions: $\mathcal{G}_v\simeq\mathbb{RP}^2$ near zero, and $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)$ has torsion.

nodes.name: Filtering function
nodes.statement:
Filtrations are usually
expressed by real functions $\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}$ called {\em filtering
functions}.

nodes.name: Multidimensional Persistence Theory
nodes.statement:
This
generalization to vector-valued functions is usually known as the
\emph{Multidimensional Persistence Theory}, where the adjective
multidimensional refers to the fact that filtering functions are
vector-valued, and has no connections with the dimensionality of
the space under study. The use of vector-valued filtering
functions in this context


enables the analysis of richer
data structures.

nodes.name: Stability of persistence diagrams (Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner, Harer)
nodes.statement:
The problem of stability in persistent homology has been studied
by Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner and Harer in \cite{CoEdHa07} for
scalar filtering functions. By using a descriptor called a
\emph{persistence diagram}, they prove that persistent Betti
numbers are stable under perturbations of filtering functions with
respect to the max-norm, provided that the considered filtering
functions are \emph{tame}.
conclusions:
persistent Betti
numbers are stable under perturbations of filtering functions with
respect to the max-norm

nodes.name: Stability of size functions
nodes.statement:
In this
context, the first stability result has been obtained for the 0th
homology in \cite{BiCeFrGiLa08}: A distance between the 0th persistent
Betti numbers, also called \emph{size functions}, has been
introduced and proven to be  stable under perturbations of
continuous vector-valued filtering functions.
conclusions:
A distance between the 0th persistent
Betti numbers, also called \emph{size functions}, has been
introduced and proven to be  stable under perturbations

nodes.name: Componentwise partial order on R^n
nodes.statement:
In this paper,
the following relations $\preceq$ and $\prec$ are defined in
$\mathbb{R}^n$: for $\vec u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)$ and $\vec v=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$,
we say $\vec u\preceq\vec v$ (resp. $\vec u\prec\vec v$) if and
only if $u_i\leq\ v_i$ (resp. $u_i<v_i$) for every index
$i=1,\dots,n$.

nodes.name: Max-norm on R^n
nodes.statement:
Moreover, $\mathbb{R}^n$ is endowed with the usual
$\max$-norm: $\left\|(u_1,u_2,\dots,u_n)\right\|_{\infty}=\max_{1\leq i\leq
n}|u_i|$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Open set Delta^+
nodes.statement:
We shall use the following notations: $\Delta^+$ will be the open
set $\{(\vec u,\vec v)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n:\vec u\prec\vec v\}$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Sublevel set
nodes.statement:
For every $n$-tuple $\vec
u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and for every function
$\vec\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}^n$, we shall denote by $X\langle\vec \varphi\preceq \vec
u\,\rangle$ the set $\{x\in X:\varphi_i(x)\leq u_i,\
i=1,\dots,n\}$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Max-norm of a continuous function
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a compact topological space and $\vec\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is a continuous function, we shall set $\|\vec \varphi\|_\infty=\max_{x\in X}\|\vec \varphi(x)\|_\infty$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Multidimensional persistent homology group
nodes.statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Let $X$ be a topological space, and $\vec \varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}^n$ a continuous
function. Let $i_*:{H}_k(X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec
u\rangle)\rightarrow {H}_k(X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec
v\rangle)$ be the homomorphism induced by the inclusion map
$i:X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec
u\rangle\hookrightarrow X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec v\rangle$ with
$\vec u\preceq\vec v$, where ${H}_k$ denotes the $k$th
homology group with coefficients in an Abelian group $G$. If $\vec u\prec\vec v$, the image of
$i_*$ is called the {\em multidimensional
$k$th persistent homology group of $(X,\vec\varphi)$ at $(\vec u, \vec
v)$}. We shall denote it by the symbol ${H}_k^{(X,\vec\varphi)}(\vec u, \vec v)$.
The function ${H}_k^{(X,\vec\varphi)}$ is called the {\em multidimensional
$k$th persistent homology group of $(X,\vec\varphi)$}.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence
nodes.statement_short: $H_k^{(X,\vec\varphi)}(\vec u,\vec v)$ is the image of the inclusion-induced map $H_k$ of sublevel set at $\vec u$ into that at $\vec v$.
nodes.label: PersHom

nodes.name: Choice of homology theory
nodes.statement: The choice of the particular homology we use is not essential in this context, in the sense that the results proven in this paper do not depend on this choice. However, while we will not further discuss this point, we recall that some important properties of persistent homology groups depend on the homology that is considered. As an example, the use of \v{C}ech homology with real coefficients allows us to assume that the function $\beta_\varphi:\Delta^+\to \mathbb{N}\cup \{\infty\}$ that takes each pair $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$ to the rank of the multidimensional $k$th persistent homology group of $(X,\vec\varphi)$ at $(\vec u, \vec v)$, is right-continuous in both its variables (cf. \cite{CeDiFeFrLa09}).
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence
nodes.statement_short: Results do not depend on the homology theory; Čech homology with real coefficients makes the rank function right-continuous.
nodes.label: rem_hom

nodes.name: Persistent homology groups of RP^2 and S^2 with |z| filtrations
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbb{RP}^2$ be the real projective plane, represented by the unordered pairs $\{p,-p\}$ of opposite points of $S^2=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3:x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}$. Let us consider the filtering functions $\varphi,\psi:\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, defined by setting
$\varphi(\{(x,y,z),-(x,y,z)\})=|z|$ and $\psi(\{(x,y,z),-(x,y,z)\})=2|z|$. Let us also consider the filtering function $\chi:S^2\to\mathbb{R}$, defined by setting $\chi(x,y,z)=|z|$. For each $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$, the persistent homology groups in degree $1$ computed at $(u,v)$ of $\varphi$, $\chi$ and $\psi$ are displayed in Figure~\ref{groups}, from left to right. The coefficients of the homology are taken in $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence
nodes.statement_short: Degree-1 persistent groups of $|z|$ and $2|z|$ on $\mathbb{RP}^2$ and $|z|$ on $S^2$, with integer coefficients.
nodes.label: ex_groups

nodes.name: Torsion prevents persistence diagrams
nodes.statement: Since we do not take coefficients in a field, the homology groups we consider have torsion, in the general case. As a consequence, they cannot be described by persistence diagrams (cf. \cite{CoEdHa07}). It follows that the classical matching distance cannot be applied, if we are interested in the information given by the torsion part of our groups.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence
nodes.statement_short: With non-field coefficients, groups have torsion, so persistence diagrams and the matching distance do not apply.

nodes.statement: Before proceeding, we recall that the term ``pseudo-distance'' means that the considered function verifies all the properties of a distance, with the possible exception of the one assuring that two elements having a vanishing distance must coincide.

nodes.name: d_T between the groups of Figure 1
nodes.statement: As a simple example, we can easily check that $d_T$ takes the value $1$ between the first two persistent homology groups represented in Figure~\ref{groups}, and the value $\infty$ between the first and the third and between the second and the third persistent homology groups represented in the same figure.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: $d_T=1$ between the two $\mathbb{RP}^2$ examples and $\infty$ between each of them and the $S^2$ example.

nodes.name: d_T is not a distance
nodes.statement: We observe that the pseudo-distance $d_T$ is not a distance. For example, we can consider the two Abelian groups $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$ (obtained by adding infinite copies of the integer numbers) and  $\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$. We can find two topological spaces $X$, $Y$ such that their homology groups in degree $1$ are these two groups, respectively. If we take the two filtering functions $\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}$, $\psi:Y\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\varphi\equiv\psi\equiv 0$, we have that $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$ and $H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)= \mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$ for any $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ with $u\ge 0$. Obviously, if $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ with $u< 0$ we get that both $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ and $H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ are the trivial group. In any case, it is easy to find a surjective homomorphism from $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ and a surjective homomorphism from $H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, so that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)=0$. However, the groups $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v), H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ are not isomorphic, for $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ with $u\ge 0$.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: $\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}$ surject onto each other, so $d_T=0$ for non-isomorphic groups.
nodes.label: rem_pd

nodes.name: Persistence diagrams for field coefficients
nodes.statement:
Let us go back to the case of filtering functions taking values in $\mathbb{R}$. In this case, if the Abelian group $G$ of homology coefficients is also a field, it is well known that
the persistent homology groups can be described by persistence diagrams, under the assumption that the topological space is triangulable (cf. \cite{CoEdHa07} for tame filtering functions, and \cite{CeDiFeFrLa09} for continuous filtering functions).

nodes.origin_citation: Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner & Harer 2007; Cerri et al. 2009
assumptions: the Abelian group $G$ of homology coefficients is also a field
conclusions: the persistent homology groups can be described by persistence diagrams

nodes.name: Persistence diagram
nodes.statement: In plain words, the persistence diagram is the collection of all points $(u,v)$ where $u$ and $v$ represent the ``birth'' and ``death'' of a homology class, varying the sub-level sets of the topological space $X$ with respect to the filtering function $\varphi:X\to \mathbb{R}$. Each one of these pairs $(u,v)$ is endowed with a multiplicity. By definition, all the pairs $(u,u)$ belong to the persistent diagram, each of them counted with infinite multiplicity.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
differentia: $u$ and $v$ represent the ``birth'' and ``death'' of a homology class
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner & Harer 2007; Cerri et al. 2009
nodes.statement_short: Points (birth, death) of homology classes with multiplicities, plus the diagonal with infinite multiplicity.

nodes.name: Matching distance
nodes.statement: The matching distance $d_{match}$ between two persistence diagrams is the infimum of the cost of a matching (i.e. a bijective correspondence) between two persistence diagrams.

nodes.name: Cost of a matching
nodes.statement: The cost of a matching $f$ is defined to be the maximum displacement of the points of the persistence diagrams, induced by $f$. Each displacement is measured by the max-norm on the real plane.

nodes.name: d_T is bounded by the matching distance
nodes.statement:
Let $X,Y$ be two triangulable spaces endowed with
two continuous functions $\varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}$, $\psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}$. Let us consider the persistent homology groups $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k$, $H^{(Y,\varphi)}_k$ with homology coefficients in a field.
Let $D_\varphi$ and $D_\psi$ be the persistent diagrams associated with the filtering functions $\varphi$ and $\psi$, respectively.
Then, for any integer $k$, $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)\le d_{match}(D_\varphi,D_\psi)$.

assumptions:
$X,Y$ be two triangulable spaces endowed with
two continuous functions $\varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}$, $\psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}$
persistent homology groups $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k$, $H^{(Y,\varphi)}_k$ with homology coefficients in a field
$D_\varphi$ and $D_\psi$ be the persistent diagrams associated with the filtering functions $\varphi$ and $\psi$
conclusions: for any integer $k$, $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)\le d_{match}(D_\varphi,D_\psi)$
nodes.statement_short: For real-valued filtrations and field coefficients, $d_T\le d_{match}$ of the persistence diagrams.
nodes.label: dtlessthandelta

nodes.name: Proof that d_T <= d_match
nodes.statement:
Since the coefficients are taken in a field, our persistent homology groups have no torsion, and they can be described by their persistent Betti numbers functions $\beta_\varphi$, $\beta_\psi$, where we set
$\beta_\varphi(u,v)=\dim {H}_k^{(X,\varphi)}(u, v)$, $\beta_\psi(u,v)=\dim {H}_k^{(Y,\psi)}(u, v)$, for $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$.
Obviously, for each $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, we have different persistent Betti numbers functions
$\beta_\varphi$ of $\varphi$ (which should be denoted
$\beta_{\varphi,k}$, say) but, for the sake of notational
simplicity,  we omit adding any reference to $k$.

Let us assume that the matching distance $d_{match}$ between our persistence diagrams takes the value $\bar \lambda$. Then, from the Representation Theorem 2.17 in \cite{CeDiFeFrLa09} (cf. also the \emph{$k$-triangle Lemma} in \cite{CoEdHa07}), it follows that for every $\lambda>\bar\lambda$ and every pair $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ the inequalities $\beta_\varphi(u-\lambda,v+ \lambda)\leq\beta_\psi(u,v)$ and $\beta_\psi(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\leq\beta_\varphi(u,v)$ hold. This fact immediately implies that for each $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$
\begin{enumerate}
\item a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\}$ exists;
\item a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\}$ exists.
\end{enumerate}
Hence $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)\le\lambda$ for any $\lambda>\bar\lambda$. This implies our thesis.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: Use the Representation Theorem (k-triangle lemma) to compare persistent Betti numbers under a $\lambda$-shift, giving the surjections required by $d_T$.

nodes.name: d_T and d_match do not coincide
nodes.statement:
Theorem~\ref{dtlessthandelta} leaves open the possibility that $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ coincide when the persistent homology groups have no torsion and hence $d_{match}$ is defined. This does not happen. Indeed, for any natural number $m\ge 2$ we can give an example for which
$d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)\le \frac{2}{m}\cdot d_{match}(D_\varphi,D_\psi)$:
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ differ: for each $m\ge2$ there is an example with $d_T\le\frac{2}{m}d_{match}$.

nodes.name: Persistence diagrams with d_T = 1 and d_match = m/2
nodes.statement: Let us consider a natural number $m\ge 2$. It is easy to define two triangulable spaces endowed with filtering functions whose persistent diagrams consist of the points  $(0,\infty),(0,m),(1,m+1),\ldots,(i,m+i),\ldots,(m,2m)$ and $(0,\infty),(0,m),(1,m+1),\ldots,(i,m+i),\ldots,(m-1,2m-1)$, respectively. Here all the points have multiplicity one. In Figure \ref{dtdelta} we can see the case $m=4$. The values of the corresponding persistent Betti number functions are displayed in Figure \ref{dtdeltavalues}. It is easy to check that in this case $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ take the value $1$ and $\frac{m}{2}$, respectively.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: Two diagrams differing by the point $(m,2m)$ give $d_T=1$ but $d_{match}=m/2$.
nodes.label: ex1

nodes.name: d_T is strictly less informative than d_match
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{dtlessthandelta} and Example~\ref{ex1} show that the pseudo-distance $d_T$ is strictly less informative than the matching distance $d_{match}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
conclusions: the pseudo-distance $d_T$ is strictly less informative than the matching distance $d_{match}$

nodes.name: Natural pseudo-distance
nodes.statement:
Let $X,Y$ be two compact topological spaces  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}^n$. The \emph{natural pseudo-distance} between the pairs $(X,\vec
\varphi)$ and $(Y,\vec \psi)$, denoted by
$\delta\left((X,\vec\varphi),(Y,\vec\psi)\right)$,  is
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] the number $\inf_{h}\|\vec
\varphi-\vec \psi \circ h\|_\infty$ where $h$ varies in the set
of all the homeomorphisms between $X$ and $Y$, if $X$ and
$Y$ are homeomorphic;
\item[(ii)] $\infty$, if $X$ and $Y$ are
not homeomorphic.
\end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\delta$ = inf over homeomorphisms $h$ of $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty$, or $\infty$ if $X,Y$ are not homeomorphic.

nodes.name: Properties of the natural pseudo-distance
nodes.statement:
We point out that the natural pseudo-distance is not a distance
because it can vanish on two distinct pairs. However, it is
symmetric, satisfies the triangular inequality, and vanishes on
two equal pairs.

nodes.name: Homeomorphism lemma for persistent homology groups
nodes.statement:
Let $X,Y$ be two homeomorphic compact topological spaces  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}^n$.
Assume that $h:X\to Y$ is a homeomorphism such that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$. Then for every pair $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$ a subgroup $S$ of $H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ and a surjective homomorphism $f:S\to  H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$ exist.
assumptions:
$X,Y$ be two homeomorphic compact topological spaces  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}^n$
$h:X\to Y$ is a homeomorphism such that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$
conclusions: for every pair $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$ a subgroup $S$ of $H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ and a surjective homomorphism $f:S\to  H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$ exist
nodes.statement_short: An $\epsilon$-close homeomorphism yields a surjection from a subgroup of $H^X(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $H^Y(\vec u-\vec\epsilon,\vec v+\vec\epsilon)$.
nodes.label: lemmahom

nodes.name: Proof of the homeomorphism lemma
nodes.statement:
The homeomorphism $h$ induces a chain isomorphism $h_*$. Obviously, $h_*$ takes cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries.  Let us consider the set $S$ of the elements of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ that contain at least one cycle whose image by $h_*$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. We claim that $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$. Indeed, if $a_1,a_2\in S$ then two cycles $\gamma_1\in a_1$, $\gamma_2\in a_2$ exist, such that $h_*(\gamma_1), h_*(\gamma_2)$ are cycles in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(\gamma_1)+h_*(\gamma_2)=h_*(\gamma_1+\gamma_2)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too. Since $\gamma_1+\gamma_2\in a_1+a_2$, it follows that the equivalence class $a_1+a_2$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the sum.

Furthermore,
if $a\in S$ then a cycle $\gamma\in a$ exists, such that $h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(-\gamma)=-h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too. Since $-\gamma\in -a$, it follows that the equivalence class $-a$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the computation of the opposite.

In summary, $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$.

Now, let us define the homomorphism $f:S\to  H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$. In the following, for each $a\in S$, let us fix a cycle $\gamma_a\in a$ such that $h_*(\gamma_a)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec \epsilon\rangle$. For every $a\in S$ we define $f(a)$ as the element of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$ that contains $h_*(\gamma_a)$ (i.e., in symbols, $[h_*(\gamma_a)]$).

We claim that $f$ is a homomorphism. In order to do that, let us consider three elements $a_1,a_2,a\in  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, such that $a_1+a_2=a$. Obviously,
$$f(a_1)+f(a_2)=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})]+[h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})+h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]$$
$$f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})].$$
Now, $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]-[h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})-h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_{a})]$.
Since $a_1+a_2=a$, a $(k+1)$-cycle $\tau$ in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$ exists, such that $\partial \tau=\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $h_*(\tau)$ is a $(k+1)$-cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Moreover, recalling that $h_*$ is a chain map, $\partial h_*(\tau)=h_*(\partial \tau)=h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$, so that $h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$ is a boundary in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$ and hence $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)]$ is the null element in $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$. This proves that $f(a_1)+f(a_2)=f(a)$.

Finally, we claim that $f$ is surjective. Indeed, let  $b\in  H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$ and $\beta\in b$, so that $\beta$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Let $\alpha$ be the cycle $\left((h_*)^{-1}\right)(\beta)=\left(h^{-1}\right)^*(\beta)$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi\circ h^{-1}-\vec\psi\|_\infty=\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $\alpha$ is a cycle in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec u\rangle$. Therefore the element $a\in  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ the cycle $\alpha$ belongs to is an element of the set $S$. Then $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})]$. Now, $\gamma_{a}$ and $\alpha$ are homologous in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$. Once again because of the inequality $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, it follows that $h_*(\gamma_{a})$ and $\beta=h_*(\alpha)$ are homologous in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence $f(a)=b$, and $f$ is proven to be surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $S$ as classes with a cycle mapped by $h_*$ into the shifted sublevel set, and $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_a)]$. Check that $S$ is a subgroup, and that $f$ is a homomorphism and surjective.

nodes.name: d_T is a lower bound for the natural pseudo-distance
nodes.statement:
Let $X,Y$ be two compact topological spaces  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}^n$. Then
$d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)\le \delta\left((X,\vec\varphi),(Y,\vec\psi)\right)$.
assumptions:
$X,Y$ be two compact topological spaces  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement_short: $d_T$ of persistent homology groups is at most the natural pseudo-distance $\delta$.
nodes.label: bound

nodes.name: Proof of the lower bound
nodes.statement:
Let us set $\bar \delta=\delta\left((X,\vec\varphi),(Y,\vec\psi)\right)$.
Because of the definition of natural pseudodistance, for each $\eta>0$ we can find a homeomorphism
$h_\eta:X\to Y$ such that $\|\vec \varphi-\vec \psi\circ h_\eta\|_\infty\le \bar\delta+\eta$.
By applying Lemma \ref{lemmahom} to both the homeomorphisms
$h_\eta:X\to Y$ and $h_\eta^{-1}:Y\to X$, we get that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)\le \bar\delta+\eta$.
Since $\eta$ can be chosen arbitrarily close to $0$, our thesis follows.
nodes.statement_short: Take near-optimal homeomorphisms $h_\eta$, apply the lemma to $h_\eta$ and $h_\eta^{-1}$, let $\eta\to0$.

nodes.name: Computable lower bound for the natural pseudo-distance
nodes.statement:
Let $X,Y$ be two compact topological spaces  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}^n$. If no surjective homomorphism exists from a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u',\vec v')\}$, then  $\delta\left((X,\vec\varphi),(Y,\vec\psi)\right)\ge \min_i\min \{u_i-u'_i,v'_i-v_i\}$.
assumptions:
$X,Y$ be two compact topological spaces  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: Y
\to \mathbb{R}^n$
no surjective homomorphism exists from a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u',\vec v')\}$
nodes.statement_short: If no subgroup of $H^X(\vec u,\vec v)$ surjects onto $H^Y(\vec u',\vec v')$, then $\delta\ge\min_i\min\{u_i-u'_i,v'_i-v_i\}$.
nodes.label: cor1

nodes.name: Proof of the computable lower bound
nodes.statement: It follows from Theorem~\ref{bound}, observing that our hypotheses easily imply that the inequality $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)\ge \min_i\min \{u_i-u'_i,v'_i-v_i\}$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Hypothesis forces $d_T\ge\min_i\min\{\cdot\}$; then apply the lower-bound theorem.

nodes.name: Stability of d_T under the max-norm
nodes.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact topological space  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: X
\to \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(X,\vec\psi)}_k\right)\le \|\vec \varphi-\vec\psi\|_\infty$.
assumptions:
$X$ be a compact topological space  endowed with
two continuous functions $\vec \varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec \psi: X
\to \mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement_short: $d_T$ between persistent groups of two filtrations of $X$ is at most their max-norm distance.
nodes.label: cor2

nodes.name: Proof of stability
nodes.statement: It follows from Theorem~\ref{bound}, observing that $\delta\left((X,\vec\varphi),(X,\vec\psi)\right)\le \|\vec \varphi-\vec\psi\|_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the lower-bound theorem with the identity homeomorphism: $\delta\le\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\|_\infty$.

nodes.name: Map pairs to directions
nodes.statement: Indeed, we can consider the continuous function $f$ taking each unordered pair $\{p,q\}\in \mathcal{G}_v$ to the direction of the line $l$ through $p$ and $q$ (note that $\{p,q\}\in \mathcal{G}_v$ implies $p\neq q$, so that $l$ is well-defined). This direction can be seen as a point in the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $f$ sending a pair to the direction of its line, a point of $\mathbb{RP}^2$.

nodes.name: Homotopy equivalence
nodes.statement: Let us observe that, for $v$ close enough to zero, the function $f:\mathcal{G}_v\to \mathbb{RP}^2$ is a homotopy equivalence (the homotopy inverse of $f$ is the function $g:\mathbb{RP}^2\to \mathcal{G}_v$ that takes each direction $w$ to the unordered pair $\{p,q\}$, where $p$ and $q$ are the points at which the line through $(0,0,0)$, having direction $w$, meets $S^2$).
nodes.statement_short: For $v$ near zero, $f$ is a homotopy equivalence with explicit inverse $g$.

nodes.name: Torsion inherited from RP^2
nodes.statement: Hence $f$ induces an isomorphism between the singular homology groups of $\mathcal{G}_v$ and $\mathbb{RP}^2$. As a consequence, since $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)$ has torsion, the persistent homology group ${H}_1^{(\mathcal{G},\varphi_\mathcal{G})}(u,v)$ has torsion, too, when $u$ is close enough to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Homology isomorphism plus torsion of $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)$ gives torsion.

nodes.name: Axioms to check
nodes.statement: The following statements hold:
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: List the pseudo-metric axioms to verify.

nodes.name: Non-negativity
nodes.statement: [$i)$] $d_T$ is non-negative by definition;
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Non-negativity holds by definition.

nodes.name: Vanishing on equal arguments
nodes.statement: [$ii)$]The equality $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k\right)=0$ is obtained by taking $\epsilon=0$ and considering the identical homomorphism $id: H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)\to H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$;
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Take $\epsilon=0$ and the identity homomorphism.

nodes.name: Symmetry
nodes.statement: [$iii)$]$d_T$ is symmetrical by definition;
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry holds by definition.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement:
[$iv)$]Assume that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)=\epsilon_1$ and $d_T\left( H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)=\epsilon_2$. Let $\eta$ be an arbitrarily small positive real number. The definition of $d_T$ implies that for each $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$ a surjective homomorphism $f$ from a subgroup $F$ of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta))$, and a surjective homomorphism $g$ from a subgroup $G$ of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta))$ onto $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$ exist. Now, we can consider the subgroup $\tilde{F}=f^{-1}(G)\subseteq  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$. Obviously, the function $g_{|G}\circ f_{|\tilde{F}}$ is a surjective homomorphism from the subgroup $\tilde{F}$ of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$.
    Analogously, we can construct a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$.
    This implies that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)\le\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+2\eta$. Since $\eta$ can be taken arbitrarily small, it follows that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)\le\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2$, so proving the triangle inequality for $d_T$.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Compose surjections to get the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Fix distances and eta
nodes.statement: Assume that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)=\epsilon_1$ and $d_T\left( H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)=\epsilon_2$. Let $\eta$ be an arbitrarily small positive real number.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$ and a small $\eta>0$.

nodes.name: Surjections from the definition
nodes.statement: The definition of $d_T$ implies that for each $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$ a surjective homomorphism $f$ from a subgroup $F$ of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta))$, and a surjective homomorphism $g$ from a subgroup $G$ of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta))$ onto $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$ exist.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: The definition of $d_T$ yields surjections $f$ and $g$.

nodes.name: Compose on the preimage subgroup
nodes.statement: Now, we can consider the subgroup $\tilde{F}=f^{-1}(G)\subseteq  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$. Obviously, the function $g_{|G}\circ f_{|\tilde{F}}$ is a surjective homomorphism from the subgroup $\tilde{F}$ of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to $f^{-1}(G)$ and compose $g\circ f$ to get a surjection.

nodes.name: Reverse direction
nodes.statement: Analogously, we can construct a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric construction from $Z$ to $X$.

nodes.name: Let eta go to zero
nodes.statement: This implies that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)\le\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+2\eta$. Since $\eta$ can be taken arbitrarily small, it follows that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)\le\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2$, so proving the triangle inequality for $d_T$.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Bound by $\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+2\eta$, then $\eta\to0$.

nodes.name: Reduce to persistent Betti numbers
nodes.statement:
Since the coefficients are taken in a field, our persistent homology groups have no torsion, and they can be described by their persistent Betti numbers functions $\beta_\varphi$, $\beta_\psi$, where we set
$\beta_\varphi(u,v)=\dim {H}_k^{(X,\varphi)}(u, v)$, $\beta_\psi(u,v)=\dim {H}_k^{(Y,\psi)}(u, v)$, for $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$.
Obviously, for each $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, we have different persistent Betti numbers functions
$\beta_\varphi$ of $\varphi$ (which should be denoted
$\beta_{\varphi,k}$, say) but, for the sake of notational
simplicity,  we omit adding any reference to $k$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: No torsion: the groups are described by persistent Betti numbers $\beta_\varphi,\beta_\psi$.

nodes.name: Betti number inequalities
nodes.statement: Let us assume that the matching distance $d_{match}$ between our persistence diagrams takes the value $\bar \lambda$. Then, from the Representation Theorem 2.17 in \cite{CeDiFeFrLa09} (cf. also the \emph{$k$-triangle Lemma} in \cite{CoEdHa07}), it follows that for every $\lambda>\bar\lambda$ and every pair $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ the inequalities $\beta_\varphi(u-\lambda,v+ \lambda)\leq\beta_\psi(u,v)$ and $\beta_\psi(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\leq\beta_\varphi(u,v)$ hold.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: Representation Theorem gives shifted Betti number inequalities for $\lambda>\bar\lambda$.

nodes.name: Surjections exist
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: The inequalities yield the two surjective homomorphisms required by $d_T$.

nodes.name: Surjection X to Y
nodes.statement: a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\}$ exists;
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: Surjection from a subgroup of $H^X(u,v)$ onto $H^Y(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Surjection Y to X
nodes.statement: a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\}$ exists.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: Surjection from a subgroup of $H^Y(u,v)$ onto $H^X(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)\le\lambda$ for any $\lambda>\bar\lambda$. This implies our thesis.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.statement_short: So $d_T\le\lambda$ for all $\lambda>\bar\lambda$.

nodes.name: Chain isomorphism
nodes.statement: The homeomorphism $h$ induces a chain isomorphism $h_*$. Obviously, $h_*$ takes cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries.
nodes.statement_short: $h$ induces a chain isomorphism $h_*$.

nodes.name: S is closed under sums
nodes.statement: Let us consider the set $S$ of the elements of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ that contain at least one cycle whose image by $h_*$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. We claim that $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$. Indeed, if $a_1,a_2\in S$ then two cycles $\gamma_1\in a_1$, $\gamma_2\in a_2$ exist, such that $h_*(\gamma_1), h_*(\gamma_2)$ are cycles in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(\gamma_1)+h_*(\gamma_2)=h_*(\gamma_1+\gamma_2)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too. Since $\gamma_1+\gamma_2\in a_1+a_2$, it follows that the equivalence class $a_1+a_2$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the sum.
nodes.statement_short: Define $S$ and claim it is a subgroup; show closure under sums.

nodes.name: Define S and claim subgroup
nodes.statement: Let us consider the set $S$ of the elements of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ that contain at least one cycle whose image by $h_*$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. We claim that $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $S$; claim it is a subgroup.

nodes.name: Sum of representing cycles
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $a_1,a_2\in S$ then two cycles $\gamma_1\in a_1$, $\gamma_2\in a_2$ exist, such that $h_*(\gamma_1), h_*(\gamma_2)$ are cycles in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(\gamma_1)+h_*(\gamma_2)=h_*(\gamma_1+\gamma_2)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too.
nodes.statement_short: Images of the sum of representatives stay in the sublevel set.

nodes.name: Closure under sum
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma_1+\gamma_2\in a_1+a_2$, it follows that the equivalence class $a_1+a_2$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the sum.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $a_1+a_2\in S$.

nodes.name: S is closed under opposites
nodes.statement:
Furthermore,
if $a\in S$ then a cycle $\gamma\in a$ exists, such that $h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(-\gamma)=-h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too. Since $-\gamma\in -a$, it follows that the equivalence class $-a$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the computation of the opposite.
nodes.statement_short: Closure of $S$ under negation.

nodes.name: S is a subgroup
nodes.statement: In summary, $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $S$ is a subgroup.

nodes.name: Define f
nodes.statement: Now, let us define the homomorphism $f:S\to  H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$. In the following, for each $a\in S$, let us fix a cycle $\gamma_a\in a$ such that $h_*(\gamma_a)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec \epsilon\rangle$. For every $a\in S$ we define $f(a)$ as the element of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$ that contains $h_*(\gamma_a)$ (i.e., in symbols, $[h_*(\gamma_a)]$).
nodes.statement_short: Define $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_a)]$ via fixed representatives.

nodes.name: f is a homomorphism
nodes.statement:
We claim that $f$ is a homomorphism. In order to do that, let us consider three elements $a_1,a_2,a\in  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, such that $a_1+a_2=a$. Obviously,
$$f(a_1)+f(a_2)=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})]+[h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})+h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]$$
$$f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})].$$
Now, $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]-[h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})-h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_{a})]$.
Since $a_1+a_2=a$, a $(k+1)$-cycle $\tau$ in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$ exists, such that $\partial \tau=\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $h_*(\tau)$ is a $(k+1)$-cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Moreover, recalling that $h_*$ is a chain map, $\partial h_*(\tau)=h_*(\partial \tau)=h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$, so that $h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$ is a boundary in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$ and hence $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)]$ is the null element in $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$. This proves that $f(a_1)+f(a_2)=f(a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $f$ is additive.

nodes.name: Expand f(a1)+f(a2)
nodes.statement:
In order to do that, let us consider three elements $a_1,a_2,a\in  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, such that $a_1+a_2=a$. Obviously,
$$f(a_1)+f(a_2)=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})]+[h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})+h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]$$
$$f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})].$$
nodes.statement_short: Write $f(a_1)+f(a_2)$ and $f(a)$ via $h_*$.

nodes.name: Difference of classes
nodes.statement: Now, $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]-[h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})-h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_{a})]$.
nodes.statement_short: Their difference is the class of $h_*$ of a cycle difference.

nodes.name: Bounding chain pushed forward
nodes.statement: Since $a_1+a_2=a$, a $(k+1)$-cycle $\tau$ in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$ exists, such that $\partial \tau=\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $h_*(\tau)$ is a $(k+1)$-cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: The bounding chain $\tau$ maps into the $\vec v+\vec\epsilon$ sublevel set.

nodes.name: Difference is null
nodes.statement: Moreover, recalling that $h_*$ is a chain map, $\partial h_*(\tau)=h_*(\partial \tau)=h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$, so that $h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$ is a boundary in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$ and hence $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)]$ is the null element in $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$. This proves that $f(a_1)+f(a_2)=f(a)$.
nodes.statement_short: So the difference is a boundary: $f$ is additive.

nodes.name: f is surjective
nodes.statement: Finally, we claim that $f$ is surjective. Indeed, let  $b\in  H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$ and $\beta\in b$, so that $\beta$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Let $\alpha$ be the cycle $\left((h_*)^{-1}\right)(\beta)=\left(h^{-1}\right)^*(\beta)$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi\circ h^{-1}-\vec\psi\|_\infty=\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $\alpha$ is a cycle in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec u\rangle$. Therefore the element $a\in  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ the cycle $\alpha$ belongs to is an element of the set $S$. Then $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})]$. Now, $\gamma_{a}$ and $\alpha$ are homologous in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$. Once again because of the inequality $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, it follows that $h_*(\gamma_{a})$ and $\beta=h_*(\alpha)$ are homologous in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence $f(a)=b$, and $f$ is proven to be surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Show $f$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Pull back a cycle
nodes.statement: Indeed, let  $b\in  H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$ and $\beta\in b$, so that $\beta$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Let $\alpha$ be the cycle $\left((h_*)^{-1}\right)(\beta)=\left(h^{-1}\right)^*(\beta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $b$, a representative $\beta$, and $\alpha=h_*^{-1}(\beta)$.

nodes.name: Preimage lies in S
nodes.statement: Given that $\|\vec\varphi\circ h^{-1}-\vec\psi\|_\infty=\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $\alpha$ is a cycle in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec u\rangle$. Therefore the element $a\in  H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ the cycle $\alpha$ belongs to is an element of the set $S$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha$ lies in the $\vec u$ sublevel set, so its class $a$ is in $S$.

nodes.name: Representatives are homologous
nodes.statement: Then $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})]$. Now, $\gamma_{a}$ and $\alpha$ are homologous in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$. Once again because of the inequality $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, it follows that $h_*(\gamma_{a})$ and $\beta=h_*(\alpha)$ are homologous in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: $h_*(\gamma_a)$ and $\beta$ are homologous in the shifted sublevel set.

nodes.name: f(a)=b
nodes.statement: Hence $f(a)=b$, and $f$ is proven to be surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $f(a)=b$.

nodes.name: Near-optimal homeomorphism
nodes.statement:
Let us set $\bar \delta=\delta\left((X,\vec\varphi),(Y,\vec\psi)\right)$.
Because of the definition of natural pseudodistance, for each $\eta>0$ we can find a homeomorphism
$h_\eta:X\to Y$ such that $\|\vec \varphi-\vec \psi\circ h_\eta\|_\infty\le \bar\delta+\eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $h_\eta$ with $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h_\eta\|_\infty\le\bar\delta+\eta$.

nodes.name: Apply the lemma both ways
nodes.statement:
By applying Lemma \ref{lemmahom} to both the homeomorphisms
$h_\eta:X\to Y$ and $h_\eta^{-1}:Y\to X$, we get that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)\le \bar\delta+\eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma on $h_\eta$ and $h_\eta^{-1}$ gives $d_T\le\bar\delta+\eta$.

nodes.name: Let eta go to zero
nodes.statement: Since $\eta$ can be chosen arbitrarily close to $0$, our thesis follows.
nodes.statement_short: Let $\eta\to0$.
